paragraphs.text: This article is a review of ball lightning sightings by scientists and other trained observers. Ball lightning is a glowing ball seen mostly in thunderstorms; it lasts a few seconds and remains unexplained. The author gathers 41 cases from eight countries, from 1868 to 2020, plus six other notable cases.

paragraphs.text: There are thousands of eyewitness reports but almost no instrument recordings, and no theory that everyone accepts. Because the event is random and brief, cameras rarely catch it, so the author argues trained observers are a promising data source.

paragraphs.text: Reported sizes range from 1.5 cm to 15 m, with most under 20 cm. Sightings lasted 1.5 to 180 seconds, with a median of 4 seconds. In this sample, 73% happened during thunderstorms, and 41% of witnesses saw a lightning strike at the same moment.

paragraphs.text: The cases vary so widely that one model struggles to fit them, so there may be several types of ball lightning. The author concludes that careful case records, physical evidence and phone or webcam footage could build a database for testing theories.

fuller.text: Ball lightning is a glowing ball, usually seen during thunderstorms, that lasts a few seconds and then vanishes, sometimes leaving damage behind. Physics still has no agreed explanation for it. This article is a historical review of 41 sightings by scientists and trained professionals, from eight countries, between 1868 and 2020.

fuller.text: The core problem is data. One search of about 12,000 sky photographs, taken nightly over ten years, found only two probable events. Large report databases never recorded who the witnesses were, so the author treats trained observers as the best available evidence.

fuller.text: The author calls the field scattered: a few people collect reports, others build theories, others run lab tests, with little coordination. The conclusion is cautiously hopeful. Cases with physical traces, plus footage from phones and webcams, could build a shared database for testing theories.

brief.text: This article collects sightings of ball lightning, a glowing ball that can appear in storms and vanish within seconds. It gathers 41 reports by scientists and other trained observers, from 1868 to 2020. Cameras almost never catch it, so careful eyewitness reports are some of the best evidence there is.

brief.text: Most sightings, 73 percent, happened during thunderstorms. Yet the balls varied widely in size, how long they lasted, and how they moved. So one simple explanation may not fit every case. The author concludes that well-recorded cases from trained observers can guide field research and help test theories.
